newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Oakfields in $6mln deal with Chinese firm.
newsitem.headline: Oakfields in $6mln deal with Chinese firm.

text.p: South African horse breeding and racing group Oakfields Thoroughbreds & Leisure Industries Ltd on Tuesday signed a $6 million joint venture deal with China's Guangzhou Jockey Club.

The move comes after President Nelson Mandela last week announced that South Africa had granted diplomatic recognition to the Peoples Republic of China and would cancel its diplomatic relations with Taiwan from December 1997.
The joint venture makes Oakfields the first South African company to announce a significant business venture with mainland China following the government's decision.
Oakfields said in a statement it would hold 40 percent of the equity in the new joint venture, the Guangzhou Jockey Club Industrial Limited, registered in Hong Kong.
The Guangzhou Jockey Club would be the majority shareholder holding the remaining equity.
The agreement would stretch over 15 years and allow for development initiatives in both countries and a substantial exchange of skills, Oakfields said.

"We believe this is one of the most important deals ever concluded between a South African company and mainland China and are proud to be at the forefront of trade with this huge potential market," managing director of Oakfields, Emmanuel Cambouris, said.
Oakfields expects to export up to 1,000 thoroughbreds per annum to the stud farm presently being established by the joint venture company in Guangzhou -- an hour's drive from Hong Kong.

"These thoroughbreds will be sold at sales in China itself, while a number will also be sold in Hong Kong and Macau," Cambouris said, adding that the export of thoroughbreds had been made possible by the acceptance of the quarantine protocol on thoroughbreds leaving the country.
In addition to advising the joint venture company on the establishment of the stud farm, Oakfields would provide extensive racing management expertise.
In exchange, Chinese personnel would be sent to South Africa to be trained in breeding and racing management.
Horse racing is in its infancy in China and the Guangzhou Jockey Club is one of the largest horse racing clubs in the country.

Giving reasons for government's decision to establish formal and diplomatic ties with China, Mandela said last week China had the world's biggest population, an economy growing at 10 percent per year, a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council, and was recognised by almost every country in the world.
South Africa's active participation in the Organisation of African Unity and the Non-Aligned Movement, whose members recognise Beijing, also influenced the decision, he said.
